title: Clinical validation of a vial wall-based dielectric barrier discharge plasma activation device for plasma-activated platelet-rich plasma preparation in osteoarthritis pain management.
abstract: Cold atmospheric plasma (CAP) has significant potential in biomedical applications. However, conventional plasma activation requires electrodes to contact a liquid directly, exposing it to the external environment. This conflicts with sterile, closed preparations required clinically. A vial wall-based dielectric barrier discharge (DBD) plasma activation device addresses this need by using standard clinical blood collection tube walls as a dielectric barrier. Electrodes contact only the tube exterior, never the liquid inside, and activation requires simply inserting the tube into the reactor chamber. Applied to platelet-rich plasma (PRP) therapy for osteoarthritis (OA), the device produced plasma-activated PRP (PA-PRP) with enhanced platelet activation, increased levels of transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β; 24%), platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF; 37%), and insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1; 32%), and broadly upregulated anti-inflammatory cytokines. In the destabilization of the medial meniscus (DMM) mouse OA model, PA-PRP treatment was associated with improved gait parameters and lower cartilage degeneration scores relative to PRP treatment. Human OA cartilage explants showed greater matrix staining after PA-PRP treatment. In an exploratory, randomized, single-blind split-body study involving three patients, PA-PRP-treated knees, compared with contralateral PRP-treated knees, showed numerically larger improvements in visual analog scale (VAS) pain score, Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) score, and effusion volume at week 15, with no adverse events during observation. These clinical observations are descriptive and hypothesis-generating, as the sample size precludes reliable efficacy or comparative safety inferences. Together, findings support device feasibility and PA-PRP use in OA and provide a rationale for adequately powered studies.

title: Strength Training in Youth: A Scoping Review with Evidence Gap Map.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Strength training has gained increasing attention in youth athletic development due to its benefits in performance and motor competence. However, a comprehensive overview of the literature examining strength training in youth populations is lacking, and research remains fragmented across sex, maturation stages, and intervention characteristics.
OBJECTIVE: To conduct a systematic scoping review with an evidence gap map of studies on strength training in youth aged 6-18 years to provide evidence-based priorities for future research and practice.
METHODS: This scoping review followed PRISMA 2020 and PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Studies involving youth athletes exposed to structured strength training interventions (e.g., resistance, bodyweight, or combined methods) were included. A systematic search of PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and SPORTDiscus was conducted up to April 20th, 2025. Data were descriptively summarized using pre-defined themes and tabulation procedures, and an evidence gap map was generated to depict how research is distributed across training variables, outcome domains, and population characteristics.
RESULTS: Out of 3770 records screened, 342 studies were included. Approximately 90% of trials assessed physical performance outcomes (e.g., strength, power, sprint speed), with limited focus on motor competence, injury prevention, or psychosocial factors. Male participants dominated the sample pool, while sex-specific analyses were uncommon. Studies involving biologically mature adolescents were scarce, and intervention durations varied widely, with numerous studies extending beyond eight weeks. A substantial proportion of studies failed to adequately report key training variables, such as frequency, intensity, supervision methods, limiting replicability, and comparability. Strength training was primarily studied in team sport contexts, especially soccer and rugby, with individual sports under-represented. Psychosocial outcomes, contextual factors (e.g., training environment), and follow-up beyond 6 months were absent in most studies. Technological and innovative approaches, including velocity-based and flywheel training, were limited to pilot studies. The evidence gap map revealed critical deficiencies in female representation, long-term follow-up, biological maturation assessment, and multidimensional outcome evaluation.
CONCLUSIONS: Current evidence indicates that youth strength training has been widely studied in relation to physical performance, injury-related outcomes, and neuromuscular development. However, important evidence gaps remain regarding biological maturity, sex-specific responses, psychosocial outcomes, long-term follow-up and context-specific applications. This scoping review identifies these gaps and highlights key priorities for future research rather than providing definitive recommendations for training practice or policy.

title: Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport and its Implications for the Foot and Ankle Surgeon.
abstract: Relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S) is a syndrome caused by low energy availability that affects multiple physiologic systems in both male and female athletes. Stress fractures of the foot and ankle are often the first signs of RED-S; therefore, it is crucial that orthopedic surgeons are aware of and able to identify this disorder. This article focuses on RED-S and provides a framework for understanding the disorder, it's relevancy to the orthopedic foot and ankle surgeon, and offers suggestions for diagnostic strategies and treatment approaches that are imperative for safe return to play.

title: Imaging and diagnosis of overuse shoulder injuries in overhead athletes.
abstract: Shoulder overuse injuries are highly prevalent among athletes participating in overhead sports such as baseball, tennis, swimming, and volleyball, where repetitive high-velocity loading imposes unique biomechanical demands on the glenohumeral complex. These injuries span a broad spectrum, including rotator cuff tears, subacromial/subdeltoid impingement, superior labrum anterior-to-posterior (SLAP) lesions, long head of the biceps tendinopathy, glenohumeral instability, internal impingement, glenohumeral internal rotation deficit (GIRD), and Little League shoulder. Accurate diagnosis requires an understanding of sport-specific biomechanics, particularly the extreme forces generated during the late cocking and early acceleration phases of throwing, which produce characteristic injury patterns such as posterosuperior partial articular-sided rotator cuff tears and type II SLAP lesions via the peel-back mechanism. Imaging plays a central role in diagnosis and management. Radiographs remain the initial study for evaluating osseous anatomy and acromial morphology. MRI is the principal modality for soft-tissue assessment, while MR arthrography offers superior sensitivity for intra-articular pathology, including labral and partial articular-sided rotator cuff tears. Musculoskeletal ultrasound provides dynamic, cost-effective evaluation of tendons and bursae, and 3D CT or zero-time echo (ZTE) MRI is essential for quantifying glenoid bone loss in the setting of instability. Because many imaging findings are present in asymptomatic athletes, careful clinical correlation is essential. This review summarizes the imaging features, diagnostic pearls, and limitations of current modalities for shoulder overuse injuries in overhead athletes.

title: Ultrasound-guided needling release combined with platelet-rich plasma injection for refractory heel pain: A case report.
abstract:
RATIONALE: Refractory heel pain is a clinically challenging condition of multifactorial origin, often complicating both diagnosis and treatment. No standard therapy exists for refractory heel pain, and clinical experience is limited. We report the efficacy of ultrasound-guided needling release of calcific deposits combined with autologous platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injection and systematic rehabilitation in a patient with refractory heel pain.
PATIENT CONCERNS: A 57-year-old self-employed female patient presented with a 3-year history of recurrent redness, swelling, and pain in the right heel, with symptoms worsening after activity. In the month prior to admission, pain had progressively worsened, limiting her ability to stand, walk, and perform daily activities.
DIAGNOSES: Refractory right heel pain (chronic calcifying Achilles tendinitis, Achilles tendinopathy, plantar fasciitis with bone spur formation).
INTERVENTIONS: The procedure involved ultrasound-guided fenestration and disruption of calcifications at the Achilles tendon insertion, followed by intralesional PRP injection and a 6-month staged rehabilitation program.
OUTCOMES: At 1 week postoperatively, Visual Analog Scale (VAS) decreased to 3, and the patient could walk independently. At 1 month, VAS was 2, and she returned to work and daily activities. At 3 months, VAS was 1, American Orthopaedic Foot and Ankle Society score improved to 90, and pain was largely resolved. The favorable outcome persisted at 6-month follow-up.
LESSONS: The combination of ultrasound-guided precise lesion management, PRP-based biological repair, and systematic rehabilitation offers a minimally invasive, safe, and effective strategy for refractory heel pain, serving as a valuable clinical reference for similar cases.

title: Sports-Related Back Pain and Injuries: From Muscle Strain to Spondylolisthesis.
abstract: Back pain is common in both the general population and young athletes, with risk increasing in sports that involve repetitive extension, rotation, and axial loading. Although most cases resolve with time, accurate diagnosis is essential to distinguish common musculoskeletal causes from more serious conditions. This article reviews key causes of athletic back pain, including muscle strain, mechanical low back pain, spondylolysis and spondylolisthesis, lumbar disc herniation, and sacroiliac joint dysfunction. It also examines diagnosis, treatment, and return to play considerations. Early recognition and appropriate management help ensure a safe and timely return to sport.

title: Clinical Assessments to Inform Return to Play Prognosis Following Acute Hamstring Injury: An Evidence-Informed Guide for Clinicians.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Rehabilitation clinicians aim to provide a return to play (RTP) prognosis following acute hamstring injury based on various clinical assessments, including subjective interview questions and physical examinations. CLINICAL QUESTION: What subjective interview questions and physical examinations should be prioritised during an initial clinical assessment following acute hamstring injury to inform RTP? KEY RESULTS: There are key subjective interview questions and physical examination findings to inform RTP prognosis following acute hamstring injury. Prolonged RTP time has been associated with athletes who: 1) recall higher pain ratings at the time of injury; 2) report pain with palpation closer to the ischial tuberosity; 3) have greater cranio-caudal length of palpable pain; 4) present with between-leg deficits of greater magnitude in maximal hip flexion active knee extension range of motion and isometric knee flexion strength in outer-range (supine with 90° hip/knee flexion) and/or mid-range (prone with 0° hip and ~15° knee flexion); and 4) experience pain during outer-range hamstring contraction. CLINICAL APPLICATION: This evidence-informed clinical commentary may help clinicians prioritise subjective interview questions and physical examinations to inform their RTP prognosis following acute hamstring injury.

title: Prevalence and associated factors of depression, anxiety, and stress among university athletes in Bangladesh.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: University athletes face substantial academic, physical, and psychosocial pressures that may heighten vulnerability to psychological distress, despite the perceived mental health benefits of sports participation. This study aimed to determine the prevalence of depression, anxiety, and stress among university athletes in Bangladesh and to examine how these conditions are associated with lifestyle and sociodemographic factors.
METHODS: This cross-sectional study was conducted from March to September 2025 among 249 university athletes aged 18-26 years at six randomly selected universities in Bangladesh. Data were collected online and in person. Psychological distress was assessed with the Depression, Anxiety, and Stress Scale-21 (DASS-21), and health-promoting lifestyle behaviors were evaluated with the Health-Promoting Lifestyle Profile II (HPLP-II). Descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, Mann-Whitney U tests, Spearman's correlations, and binary logistic regression analyses were conducted.
RESULTS: The prevalence of depression, anxiety, and stress was 42.6%, 42.6%, and 43.8%, respectively. Depression, anxiety, and stress were significantly associated with relationship status, fatigue, socioeconomic status, smoking, sleep duration, sports participation frequency, and satisfaction with sports (all p < 0.05). Participants with depression, anxiety, and stress had significantly lower scores across all HPLP-II domains (all p < 0.01). Higher physical activity was independently associated with lower odds of depression (OR = 0.462, 95% CI: 0.286-0.746), anxiety (OR = 0.756, 95% CI: 0.677-0.845), and stress (OR = 0.773, 95% CI: 0.677-0.882). Better stress management and stronger interpersonal relationships were also significantly associated, whereas other factors were not.
CONCLUSIONS: Depression, anxiety, and stress were highly prevalent among university athletes in Bangladesh and strongly associated with modifiable lifestyle factors. These findings support integrated, athlete-centered mental health strategies emphasizing physical activity, stress management, and psychosocial support. However, the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference and determination of the directionality of these associations.
CLINICAL TRIAL NUMBER: Not applicable.

title: Comparative physiological responses to self-paced exercise in men across age-training status: effort distribution, cerebral-muscle oxygenation and neuromuscular performance.
abstract: To compare self-paced cycling performance, effort distribution, and associated neuromuscular and physiological responses across three age-training phenotypes. Twenty-eight healthy men were classified as young trained (YT, n = 8; 26.3 ± 6.9 y), older trained (OT, n = 11; 57.5 ± 3.4 y), or young untrained (YU, n = 9; 24.8 ± 5.3 y). Participants completed a 25-min self-paced cycling time trial comprising five 4.5-min lower-intensity sections, each followed by a 30-s maximal sprint. Power output, heart rate (HR), rating of perceived exertion, blood lactate, core and skin temperature, cerebral and muscle tissue oxygenation, and pre/post knee-extensor neuromuscular function were assessed. Total distance differed between groups (P = 0.037), with OT cycling further than YU (12.87 ± 1.32 vs. 11.48 ± 0.89 km; mean difference 1.40 km, 95% CI 0.35-2.44; adjusted P = 0.035), whereas OT and YT did not differ. During lower-intensity sections, OT produced greater absolute power than YU (mean difference 51.8 W, 95% CI 18.8-84.7; adjusted P = 0.012). Sprint-power variability was lower in OT than YU (7.8 ± 6.0 vs. 28.4 ± 18.5%; adjusted P = 0.030). Peak HR was lower in OT than both younger groups. Voluntary activation showed no significant group x time interaction (P = 0.062), and NIRS responses showed no significant group x stage interactions. Older trained men achieved self-paced cycling performance comparable with young trained men and greater than young untrained men, characterised by sustained lower-intensity power and more stable sprint output despite a lower peak HR.

title: Adaptive training load optimization for sprinters via offline reinforcement learning and multi-modal physiological feedback.
abstract: Elite sprint training requires daily adjustment of training load to balance performance adaptation and fatigue, yet physiological monitoring does not necessarily translate into a specific next-session prescription. This study formalizes daily sprint training prescription as a finite-horizon Markov Decision Process and develops an adaptive load-optimization framework that couples multi-modal physiological feedback with offline reinforcement learning (RL). A 19-dimensional state fusing autonomic, neuromuscular, endocrine, subjective, and load-aggregate signals is encoded by a dual-tower network [a one-dimensional convolutional neural network-Transformer temporal branch and a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) static branch] over an action space of 62 admissible training-type/intensity/volume combinations. A composite reward penalizes overreaching while rewarding short-term gain, longitudinal adaptation, and acute-to-chronic workload ratio conformity. The policy is learned by conservative off-policy training on retrospective data, evaluated through the Fitted Q-Evaluation (FQE) and Doubly Robust (DR) estimators, and presented to coaches as the three leading candidate actions, with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) values used to explain the model's preferences among the candidate actions. In a 12-week single-center retrospective comparison of 70 national-level sprinters (35 men and 35 women; 100 m personal best (PB) ≤ 11.20 s for men or ≤ 12.50 s for women), grouped by whether their squad had adopted the tool (n = 35 RL-guided) or continued classical block periodisation (n = 35 control), the RL-guided cohort demonstrated between-cohort differences of +0.240 s in 100 m [95% confidence interval (CI) +0.128 to +0.352; p < 0.001, d = 1.00], +0.104 s in 30 m (p < 0.001, d = 1.00) and +2.17 cm in countermovement jump (p < 0.001, d = 1.01). Zero algorithmically defined sustained multi-indicator fatigue/load events were observed in the RL-guided cohort vs. seven in the control cohort (1.43 per 1,000 athlete-days); these events should not be interpreted as clinically diagnosed overtraining syndrome. Off-policy evaluation yielded exploratory point estimates whose precision remains unknown because uncertainty intervals were not calculated. These observational findings describe associations with an RL-guided, coach-in-the-loop workflow and do not establish a causal effect of the RL policy.

title: Smartphone Accelerometer Assessment of HRV: Concurrent Agreement of the KubiosHRV App.
abstract: Heart rate variability (HRV) is widely used to monitor athlete recovery and adaptation. Recent technological advances have enabled HRV assessment through smartphone applications without the need for external devices. This study aimed to assess the concurrent agreement between the accelerometer-based HRV measurement feature of the KubiosHRV app and the Polar H10 in supine, seated, and standing positions. A total of 52 participants (30 males and 22 females) across performance tiers 0-4 completed a 2 min resting recording, with the first minute discarded and the second minute analysed in each position. HRV was measured simultaneously using a Polar H10 chest strap and the accelerometer-based feature of the KubiosHRV app on an iPhone 14. The analysed variables included Mean RR, RMSSD, SDNN, LF power, HF power, SD1, and SD2. Data were automatically processed by the KubiosHRV app and manually extracted into a database. Results showed excellent intraclass correlation coefficients (≥0.985) and small magnitudes of error for time-domains and non-linear variables in the three analysed positions with the reference criterion. Frequency-domain variables showed larger error estimates. Bland-Altman analysis showed no evidence of proportional bias across the measurement range (p > 0.05). These findings suggest that, during 1 min recordings, the accelerometer-based feature of the KubiosHRV app showed strong concurrent agreement with the Polar H10 for time-domain variables and acceptable agreement for selected non-linear variables across positions. Therefore, it may represent a practical alternative for routine monitoring of these HRV metrics when external hardware is unavailable.

title: Open and closed-chain shoulder joint position sense: inter-day reliability and normative profiles in male contact sport athletes.
abstract: The purpose was to determine inter-day reliability and normative values for open and closed-chain shoulder joint position sense (JPS). Male contact and collision sport athletes (18-40 years) participated in two study phases. Sixteen athletes completed open- and closed-chain JPS tests on two occasions (2-9 days apart) to determine inter-day reliability. Twenty-eight athletes completed the same protocol on one occasion to establish normative profiles. Open-chain JPS was assessed in a standing position using shoulder flexion to pre-defined angles with a laser pointer (55°, 90° and 125° of humerothoracic flexion; no haptic target); closed-chain JPS was assessed in a push-up position by reproducing target positions (chest lowered onto a hurdle at 16.5 cm [low] or 30.5 cm [high]; an initial haptic target). Three-dimensional kinematics quantified repositioning errors. Intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) and standard error of measurement (SEM) were calculated for reliability. Pearson correlations were calculated between open and closed-chain errors. Open-chain tests demonstrated moderate reliability across both arms (ICCs = 0.71-0.74), with better reliability on the dominant limb (ICCs = 0.68-0.90) compared to the non-dominant (ICCs = 0.43-0.55). SEM values ranged from 0.70 to 2.03°. Closed-chain tests showed poor reliability at the high target (ICC = 0.49) but good reliability at the low target (ICC = 0.81, SEM = 10.2 mm). Normative data indicated greater repositioning errors at low targets in open-chain tasks and at high targets in closed-chain tasks. Correlations between open- and closed-chain errors were weak to absent. Open-chain JPS testing demonstrated acceptable reliability, whereas closed-chain reliability was dependent on target height. The two tasks appear to assess distinct aspects of proprioception. The open-chain test reflects predominantly single-joint (glenohumeral) position sense, whereas the closed-chain test reflects multi-joint, composite position sense. These findings establish initial reference values for JPS in male contact athletes.

title: Associations between countermovement jump impulse and running kinetics following ACL reconstruction.
abstract: Persistent deficits in lower-limb loading are commonly observed following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) and may influence running biomechanics. Countermovement jump (CMJ) impulse can provide a phase-specific measure of force-time characteristics to reflect limb loading capacity; however, its relationship with running kinetics remains unclear. This study aimed to quantify phase-specific CMJ impulse following ACLR and examine associations with vertical ground reaction force (vGRF) metrics during treadmill running at the return-to-running phase. Forty-two participants performed three unilateral and bilateral CMJs on dual force plates and ran at 8 km/hr on an instrumented treadmill. Concentric, eccentric braking, and landing impulses were calculated. Running variables included weight acceptance rate, weight acceptance peak force, and maximum applied force. Inter-limb differences were assessed using Wilcoxon/paired t-tests. Impulse-vGRF relationships were analysed using Pearson/Spearman correlations and multiple linear regression. The ACLR limb exhibited significant deficits across all unilateral and bilateral CMJ phases, except for unilateral landing impulse. Deficits were greatest for unilateral concentric impulse (Δ1.3Ns·kg-0.67, d = 1.49, p < 0.001). Maximum applied force limb symmetry index (LSI) was explained by unilateral concentric impulse LSI (adjusted R2 = 0.25, p < 0.001). Maximum applied force of the affected limb was explained by unilateral concentric impulse (adjusted R2 = 0.38, p < 0.001). Weight acceptance peak force of the affected limb was explained by unilateral concentric and landing impulses (adjusted R2 = 0.37, p < 0.001). No meaningful relationships were observed for eccentric impulses or weight acceptance rate metrics. These findings indicate that jump impulse testing may provide clinically relevant indicators of running kinetics.

title: Sex- and Sport-Specific Differences in Mobility and Muscle Function Characteristics in Division I Athletes.
abstract: Gonzalez, AM, Sell, KM, Mangine, GT, Ghigiarelli, JJ, Gerland, RW, Deveaux, B, DiMonda, R, Prendergast, JM, and Bentivegna, J. Sex- and sport-specific differences in mobility and muscle function characteristics in Division I athletes. J Strength Cond Res 40(12): 1569-1580, 2026-The purpose of the present investigation was to compare sex- and sport-specific differences in joint mobility, bilateral asymmetry, and muscle function characteristics among Division I collegiate athletes. Two hundred and seventy six male (n = 144) and female (n = 132) athletes from 7 sports completed a comprehensive, preseason assessment battery. Mobility assessments included hip, shoulder, ankle, thoracic, and pelvic range-of-motion, as well as sit-and-reach performance. Muscle function assessments included measures of vertical jump height, hand grip strength, and hip abduction/adduction strength. Measures were analyzed using mixed-model analyses of variance to examine effects of sex, sport, and limb dominance. Clear sex- and sport-specific differences were observed across multiple mobility measures. Female athletes demonstrated significantly greater joint mobility than male athletes across several anatomical regions (p < 0.001-0.03; η2p = 0.02-0.16), whereas male athletes display superior muscle function performance across strength (p < 0.001-0.02; η2p = 0.06-0.3) and vertical jump (p < 0.001, η2p = 0.50) measures. Mobility asymmetries varied substantially by sport and joint, while strength asymmetries were minimal across groups. These findings provide sex- and sport-specific reference data and reinforce the importance of individualized interpretation of mobility and muscle function assessments in athletic populations.

title: Nationwide Trends, Regional Variation and Seasonality of Surgically Treated Achilles Tendon Rupture in Japan: An Analysis of Descriptive Epidemiological Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Achilles tendon rupture (ATR) is a common foot and ankle injury among physically active adults. Nationwide evidence on long-term trends, regional variation, seasonality and COVID-19-related changes in Japan is limited. We characterised the surgical burden of ATR using a national administrative database.
METHODS: We conducted a nationwide descriptive epidemiological study using aggregated data from the National Database of Health Insurance Claims and Specific Health Checkups (NDB) Open Data for fiscal years (FY) 2014-2022. Temporal trends, prefectural variation, seasonal patterns and pandemic-associated changes were examined using counts, population-based rates and quasi-Poisson regression.
RESULTS: During FY2014-2019, approximately 11,200 surgeries were performed annually (8.8 per 100,000 person). In FY2020, incidence declined to 5.9 per 100,000 (incidence rate ratio [IRR] 0.67), with greater reductions among adults aged 30-59 (61%-64% of baseline) and, after age adjustment, among women (IRR 0.61 vs. 0.71 in men; interaction p = 0.039). Incidence partially recovered in FY2021-2022 (7.6 per 100,000; IRR 0.86). Incidence varied across the 47 prefectures (pre-COVID range: 5.0-16.7 per 100,000), and all declined in FY2020 (mean ratio 0.69). Monthly counts peaked in spring-early summer and were higher in spring than in winter (p = 0.018).
CONCLUSIONS: The incidence of surgically treated ATR in Japan was stable before the COVID-19 pandemic, declined markedly in FY2020 and partially recovered thereafter, with the largest reductions among working-age adults and women. Regional variation and seasonality were preserved. These findings can inform surgical and rehabilitation service planning.

title: Time-Efficient Reactive Agility Training Improves Motor and Cognitive Components of Reactive Agility in Open- and Closed-Skill Athletes: A 6-Week Intervention Study.
abstract: Reactive agility (RA), the ability to respond to external stimuli with whole-body movements as quickly and precisely as possible, is crucial for many sports, particularly open-skill sports, and is influenced by both motor and cognitive abilities. This study aims to investigate which of the underlying components of RA is most improved through RA training, whether prior experience with RA movements influences the rate of improvement, and whether a time-ecological approach also leads to improvements. Assessments included 19 open-skill and 26 closed-skill athletes with different competitive backgrounds. RA training was carried out once a week for six weeks with each session lasting 20 minutes. Pre- and post-assessments were conducted for RA (Random Star Run), change-of-direction (t-Test), and cognitive performance (Stroop test). Baseline differences between open- and closed-skill athletes and performance level were evaluated using 2 × 2 ANOVA. Intervention effects were calculated using repeated measures ANOVA. Open-skill athletes were significantly faster within the RA task than closed-skill athletes (p = 0.017; F = 6.247; η2 p = 0.132). Both groups improved significantly across all outcome measures (p < 0.05; RA and both underlying properties) with no interaction effects of group × time (p > 0.05). One weekly 20-min training session is sufficient to improve RA, and selected motor and cognitive performance parameters. Prior experience, based on regular participation in open-skill sports, seems to be associated with higher RA performance but does not moderate training adaptations, as both groups improved similarly in RA and the underlying motor and cognitive functions.

title: Enhancing Sleep in NCAA Division I Athletes: A Study of Sleep Extension Feasibility.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sleep extension has been shown to improve varied aspects of athletic performance in collegiate athletes. Such studies have been conducted in small cohorts in controlled settings utilizing obsolete monitoring technology. The feasibility of sleep extension has not been evaluated in a broader cohort of collegiate athletes with modern monitoring technology.
HYPOTHESIS: Sleep extension may not be feasible in National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) Division I athletes.
STUDY DESIGN: Crossover study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 3.
METHODS: Baseline sleep data were collected from NCAA Division I athletes (women's soccer, men's soccer, baseball, and football) during a 2-week period. Subjects were then instructed to extend their total sleep time to 10 hours per night for 2 weeks. All sleep baseline and extension data were collected in the offseason, remote from school examinations. WHOOP bands recorded all sleep metrics. Data were analyzed using paired-samples t tests and Wilcoxon signed rank tests.
RESULTS: A total of 50 subjects (14 female, 36 male) participated. The study compared total sleep time (hours) and sleep consistency (percent) - the stability of sleep-wake schedule over time, between baseline and sleep extension phases. Sample size varied for both metrics, ranging from 46 to 49 participants, respectively. There was a statistically significant increase in sleep consistency during the sleep extension phase (baseline, 60.09 ± 12.6%; extension, 64.42 ± 12.4%; P = 0.02). However, total sleep time showed no significant difference between the 2 phases (baseline, 7.63 ± 0.88 hours; extension, 7.51 ± 0.88 hours; P = 0.27).
CONCLUSION: Extension efforts improved sleep consistency but did not significantly impact total sleep time suggesting that a sleep extension intervention can enhance sleep consistency in NCAA Division I athletes but does not significantly impact total sleep time. Sleep extension may be challenging for collegiate athletes given the time-intensive demands of both academics and sports. While sleep extension may be feasible in professional sports, it does not appear to be so in the college setting.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: While the sleep extension intervention improved sleep consistency, it did not improve total sleep time, questioning the feasibility of sleep extension in collegiate sports.

title: Mechanisms and Movement Patterns of Ankle Sprain Injuries in Male Handball: A Video-Based Analysis.
abstract: Ankle sprains are among the most common injuries in handball. However, evidence on high-risk movements and injury circumstances is scarce. This video analysis study investigated the situational characteristics of athletes sustaining ankle sprains. A systematic web search (YouTube, Google News) identifying video recordings of ankle injuries in male handball players was performed. Two independent examiners extracted sample information (e.g., age, height, weight, position), mechanism of injury (direct, indirect, non-contact), movement pattern (landing, change of direction/CoD, running, shuffle, step/lunge, other), action speed, focus of visual attention, and time of injury. In addition to descriptive statistics, χ2-tests were used to examine variable associations. A total of 118 video-recorded injuries were obtained. Most sprains were direct contact injuries (n = 72, 61.0%), and the most frequent movement patterns were landing (n = 46), running (n = 15), step/lunge (n = 14), and CoD (n = 13). While direct injuries occurred primarily during landing (43%), non-contact mechanisms (85%) were, by far, the main cause of injury during change of Direction movements (p < 0.01). In the majority of cases, movement speed was moderate (n = 63) and visual attention was directed to the ball (n = 56). Landings are the most frequent cause of ankle sprains in male handball players. Although the largest share, particularly landing-related injuries, results from direct contact, non-contact sprains display a unique pattern as they mostly occur during CoD. Conditioning coaches and health personnel may consider this disparity when designing preventive measures.

title: Tired of Thinking? Think Again! A Longitudinal Experience-Sampling Study of Bidirectional Dynamics Between Rumination and Mental Fatigue in Athletes.
abstract: Recovery days are intended to support psychological and physical recovery, yet repetitive sport-related thinking may interfere with this process. This four-week experience-sampling study examined the dynamic interplay between rumination and mental fatigue during rest days in competitive athletes, as well as the moderating roles of perfectionistic concerns and perfectionistic strivings. A total of 134 athletes completed repeated rest-day assessments of rumination and mental fatigue, with perfectionism measured at baseline using a sport-adapted version of the FMPS-Brief. Continuous-time structural equation modelling revealed significant bidirectional coupling between rumination and mental fatigue, supporting a self-reinforcing dynamic in which rumination fuels fatigue, and accumulated fatigue heightens the likelihood of further rumination, creating a 'vicious cycle'. The rumination → mental fatigue pathway was stronger than the reverse, underscoring the critical importance of mental rest and psychological recovery in sport. Perfectionistic concerns significantly moderated this association, suggesting that athletes high in evaluative self-criticism may be more vulnerable to the rumination-fatigue cycle, whereas perfectionistic strivings did not exert a moderating effect. These findings advance a process-oriented understanding of psychological recovery in athletes and may inform future research on how short-term rumination-fatigue dynamics contribute to longer-term maladaptive recovery patterns, including burnout risk. Interventions targeting repetitive negative thinking, such as mindfulness-, cognitive-behavioral-, or acceptance-based approaches, may help athletes preserve psychological recovery under performance demands.

title: Immediate Return or Overnight Stay? Sleep Responses by Postmatch Travel Strategy and Match Participation in Professional Football.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Late European away fixtures can disrupt sleep, but the influence of immediate return versus overnight stay, and whether responses differ by match participation, remains unclear.
HYPOTHESIS: Postmatch travel strategy would influence sleep quality and duration across the prematch, match, and subsequent nights, with responses moderated by match participation.
STUDY DESIGN: Observational repeated-measures field study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 3.
METHODS: A total of 19 outfield English Premier League players were monitored across 10 European away fixtures (5 immediate return and 5 overnight stay). Self-reported sleep quality (1 to 7) and sleep duration were recorded on the prematch, match, and subsequent nights. Fixed-effects models examined condition, time, and match participation, with standard errors clustered by player.
RESULTS: Sleep quality was lower than prematch baseline on the match and subsequent nights (both β = -0.62 arbitrary units [AU]; P < 0.01; g = -0.63). After overnight stay, sleep quality improved from the match to the subsequent night in players who participated and those who did not (β = 0.69 and 0.63 AU; 95% CIs, 0.37-0.90 and 0.47-0.91; P < 0.01), whereas no change occurred after immediate return. Across participation groups, sleep duration was lower after overnight stay than immediate return on the match night (β = -1.94 hours; P < 0.01; g = -1.26) and subsequent night (β = -1.02 hours; P = 0.02; g = -0.67). However, after overnight stay, sleep duration increased between these nights by 1.45 hours in participants and 1.43 hours in nonparticipants (P < 0.01), with no significant change after immediate return. Participation moderated sleep duration on both postfixture nights (β = 1.27 and 1.64 hours; P ≤ 0.04; g = 0.82 and 1.07).
CONCLUSION: Neither travel strategy was uniformly superior. Overnight stay was associated with poorer absolute sleep duration but a clearer next-night rebound in sleep quality and duration.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Postmatch travel should be planned case by case, considering itinerary, next-day demands, and individual match exposure rather than applying a single team-wide policy.

title: Performance and Physiological Responses to Strength Training Programs in Elite Judo Athletes.
abstract: Campos, BT, Rodrigues, JGdS, Cal Abad, CC, Bachi, ALL, dos Santos, CMM, Tritto, AC, Kons, RL, Penna, EM, and Prado, LS. Performance and physiological responses to strength training programs in elite judo athletes. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study compared the effects of 2 short-term strength training models, block planning (BP) and undulating planning (UP), on performance, physiological, and perceptual responses in elite judo athletes. We hypothesized that BP would induce greater physiological strain due to the concentration of training stimuli. Eighteen judokas (14 men and 4 women) were randomly assigned to BP (n = 9) or UP (n = 9) for 4 weeks, performing 6 weekly strength sessions alongside technical-tactical training. Performance outcomes included countermovement jump (CMJ), muscle power (back squat and bent-over row), and the Special Judo Fitness Test (SJFT). Monitoring variables included internal load, heart rate variability (HRV), and well-being, while physiological markers included creatine kinase, tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), and cortisol. Data were analyzed using 2-way repeated-measures ANOVA (p < 0.05). Both groups improved SJFT performance (p < 0.01), with no between-group differences. Block planning increased lower-limb peak power (p = 0.01; d = 0.90), whereas UP showed no meaningful change. Upper-limb power and CMJ did not change in either group. Internal load showed different temporal patterns between models. Block planning presented higher HRVcv values (p = 0.04), indicating greater autonomic perturbation. Creatine kinase and TNF-α increased over time in both groups (p ≤ 0.05), while cortisol showed an interaction without clear post hoc differences. In conclusion, BP improved lower-limb power but increased physiological strain, whereas UP elicited similar judo-specific improvements with lower recovery demands. These findings highlight the importance of training organization for balancing performance and recovery in elite judo athletes.

title: Body recomposition in adults: mechanisms, modulators, and practical algorithms for simultaneous skeletal muscle mass gain and fat mass loss.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Body recomposition is the concurrent increase in fat-free mass (FFM) or skeletal muscle mass and decrease in fat mass (FM) within the same intervention period. Although hypertrophy is commonly pursued in energy surplus and FM loss in energy deficit, controlled trials indicate that recomposition can occur when progressive resistance training (PRT), adequate protein intake, and an appropriate energy prescription are combined.
METHODS: We conducted a structured narrative review of randomised trials, meta-analyses, and selected mechanistic studies in adults, with emphasis on FFM, FM, strength, and performance outcomes. Device heterogeneity was considered when interpreting evidence, with greatest weight placed on four-compartment and dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) outcomes.
RESULTS: PRT combined with higher protein intake, typically ~1.6-2.4 g/kg/day and higher relative intakes during energy restriction or leanness, is the most consistent strategy for recomposition. Effects are largest in untrained individuals and those with higher adiposity, smaller in trained or lean athletes, and still feasible in older adults when anabolic resistance is addressed with supervised PRT and sufficient protein. Moderate deficits, carbohydrate allocation around key sessions, sleep, and recovery support FFM retention or accretion while facilitating FM loss. Practical applications: Programmes should pair progressive overload with protein-centred diets, modest energy deficits, and periodic monitoring of body composition and performance.
CONCLUSIONS: Body recomposition is feasible but context-dependent; expected changes are generally modest in trained or lean populations and require individualised adjustment.
journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

title: Increased patellar tendon size and stiffness are associated with reduced knee extensor rate of torque development after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction with bone-patellar tendon-bone graft.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Knee extensor weakness persists long-term following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) with a bone-patellar tendon-bone (BPTB) autograft, yet the contribution of donor patellar tendon morphology and mechanical properties to these deficits remains unclear. The purpose of this study was to determine whether donor patellar tendon properties were associated with knee extensor rate of torque development (RTD) and peak torque following ACLR with BPTB autograft.
METHODS: Twenty-five individuals (18.4 ± 2.8 years) underwent ultrasonography of the patellar tendon and isometric knee extensor strength testing approximately 3-4.5 months postsurgery. B-mode ultrasound and shear wave elastography were collected bilaterally to assess patellar tendon cross-sectional area (CSA), thickness and regional stiffness.
RESULTS: The donor patellar tendon was significantly larger (p < 0.001), thicker (p < 0.001) and stiffer (p = 0.001) than the uninvolved tendon. Patellar tendon CSA, thickness and stiffness were not associated with peak torque (p = 0.146 to 0.853); however, several properties were identified as negative predictors of RTD. Medial patellar tendon stiffness was the strongest negative predictor of RTD (R 2 = 0.276, p = 0.007), with stiffness, CSA and thickness collectively explaining 40.8% of the variance in RTD (p = 0.010).
CONCLUSIONS: Patellar tendon adaptations after graft harvest were negatively associated with RTD but not peak torque. While not causally established, these findings provide a potential target for rehabilitation aimed at restoring explosive strength after ACLR.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III.

title: Pelvic floor knowledge and unhealthy habits related in female athletes: a cross-sectional study.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To describe pelvic floor (PF)-related knowledge and unhealthy habits among female athletes, and to examine their associations with PF dysfunction (PFD) symptoms, sports characteristics, academic level and help seeking attitudes.
METHODS: A total of 538 female athletes (36.7 ± 11.3 years) completed an anonymous online questionnaire covering age, academic level, sports experience, unhealthy PF-related habits, PFD symptoms, professional healthcare-seeking attitude and knowledge about urinary incontinence (UI), anorectal incontinence (ARI), pelvic organ prolapse (POP) and female sexual dysfunction (FSD). Adequate knowledge was considered as ≥70% correct responses.
RESULTS: Female athletes demonstrated adequate knowledge regarding UI, ARI and POP, but insufficient knowledge about FSD (52.6%). Several PFD symptoms were associated with lower knowledge levels and a higher number of unhealthy habits compared with athletes without these symptoms (p<0.05). Younger athletes showed lower knowledge about ARI (p=0.033) and POP (p=0.003), while older athletes showed lower knowledge about FSD (p<0.001). Athletes who rejected professional healthcare showed lower knowledge across all PFD domains (p<0.05).
CONCLUSIONS: Female athletes reporting symptoms suggestive of PFD showed lower levels of knowledge and a higher number of unhealthy PF habits compared with those without symptoms. Although athletes generally demonstrated an appropriate level of knowledge regarding PFD, important gaps were observed in the FSD domain and in unhealthy toileting and sport-related habits, particularly among athletes without university studies. Differences in knowledge were also observed according to age and healthcare-seeking attitudes, highlighting areas that may be considered in future educational initiatives.

title: Adhesive and Antibacterial Bio-Based Hydrogel for Human Voice Recognition and Osteoarthritis Recovery Monitoring.
abstract: Conductive hydrogels derived from natural polysaccharides hold great promise for next generation wearable electronics owing to their intrinsic biocompatibility, adhesiveness, and tunable mechanical properties. However, realizing amylum-based hydrogels with simultaneously high stretchability, sensitivity, strong adhesion and antibacterial performance remains a significant challenge. Herein, a multifunctional ionic hydrogel, marked as PAPC4 hydrogel, composed of polyacrylamide (PAAm), amylum and phenol-modified chitosan is developed via a one-pot synthesis strategy. The hydrogel exhibits exceptional stretchability (up to 1605%), short response time (16.1 ms), high optical transparency (96%), strong adhesion (43.2 kPa on PVC) and pronounced antibacterial activity. Cytotoxicity assays, live/dead staining, and subcutaneous implantation supported its biocompatibility under the tested conditions, while bacterial assays demonstrated activity against Escherichia coli. As a strain sensor, PAPC4 detected joint movements and throat vibrations during speech. It also recorded differences in knee movement among control, osteoarthritis, and treated osteoarthritis groups in rats. These results support the use of this chitosan-starch composite hydrogel in wearable motion sensing and rehabilitation monitoring.

title: Arthroscopic technique for anterior cruciate ligament repair augmented with an internal brace: Current technique.
abstract: Primary anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) repair serves as a joint-preserving surgical option for carefully selected acute proximal ACL tears (Sherman Type I and II) presenting within 4 weeks of injury. The proximal ACL stump is secured using high-strength FiberWire sutures, which are passed through the adjustable loop of a cortical button incorporating a FiberTape suture that acts as an internal brace. The distal ends of the repair sutures and internal brace tape are subsequently fixed to the proximal anteromedial tibial cortex using an externally attachable button system. Compared with conventional ACL reconstruction, primary repair aims to preserve the native ACL stump and its proprioceptive mechanoreceptors, which may theoretically maintain dynamic stability and physiological knee kinematics while avoiding donor-site morbidity. The internal brace acts as a secondary mechanical stabilizer during the early healing phase, sharing loads to prevent gap formation and protect the biological repair during early motion. This technical note describes patient selection criteria, portal placement, precise construct assembly, differential knee-flexion tensioning, and a criteria-based postoperative rehabilitation protocol.

title: The Ankle's Roll in Landing: Insights Into ACL Injury Biomechanics.
abstract: Noncontact ACL injuries typically occur within the first 40 milliseconds after ground contact, before voluntary neuromuscular responses can alter joint loading. This study quantified whether early ankle and foot mechanics during single-leg landing are associated with knee biomechanics within an ACL injury-relevant timeframe. Forty-one recreationally active adults performed a horizontal-to-vertical single-leg hop, while kinematics and ground reaction forces were recorded. Gradient-boosted decision tree models with participant-wise leave-one-subject-out cross-validation and nested feature selection were used to predict knee outcomes from ankle mechanics and participant descriptors. Knee-flexion displacement demonstrated the strongest predictive performance (R2 = .430), with greater ankle dorsiflexion at initial contact associated with reduced knee-flexion displacement. Across its interquartile range, initial-contact dorsiflexion was associated with a 4.36° reduction in predicted knee-flexion displacement. Knee-extensor yield impulse demonstrated the next-highest R2 (.334), with greater magnitude early plantarflexor yield impulse associated with greater knee-extensor yield impulse (0.0160 N·m·s·kg-1 across its interquartile range). Frontal-plane knee outcomes and peak vertical ground reaction force were poorly predicted. These findings identify initial-contact ankle-dorsiflexion and early plantarflexor yield impulse as distal variables associated with selected sagittal-plane knee outcomes during early landing.

title: FoRist: Three-DoF Soft Wearable Robot for Forearm and Wrist Assistance.
abstract: The growing population of elderly individuals affected by musculoskeletal and neurological diseases experiences multijoint functional impairment, and individuals with compromised forearm and wrist function can lose independence and quality of life. However, most wearable robotic devices provide assistance for a single degree of freedom (DoF) and restrict other joint movements because decoupling multijoint kinematics remains challenging. This article introduces FoRist, a lightweight three-DoF soft wearable robot designed for forearm and wrist assistance. FoRist assists wrist ulnar/radial deviation, wrist extension/flexion, and forearm pronation/supination through a spring blade-based active-passive hybrid actuation mechanism using three motors. It integrates compact rail structures, soft tension transfer mechanisms, and a flexible twisted string actuation mechanism to assist forearm-wrist motion while preserving freedom of movement in the neighboring hand and elbow joints. The local wearable structure at the wristband rail-slider engagement has a maximum thickness of 16 mm. Its personalized usability features, including bioanatomical analysis-driven customization and user-friendly donning/doffing, support application to individuals with forearm and wrist impairments. User tests with stroke survivors showed that wearing FoRist increased the achievable range of motion and output torque across the forearm and wrist movements compared with unassisted movement. In a two-participant test of a simulated food-preparation sequence involving opening a jar, scooping jam, and spreading jam on bread, FoRist assistance increased task-relevant wrist motion and was associated with lower maximum shoulder abduction. These preliminary results support FoRist's feasibility and usability in short-term laboratory use. With its compact three-DoF architecture, low distal mass, and personalized fit, FoRist offers a promising avenue for extending rehabilitation training beyond clinical settings and has the potential to enhance independence and functional performance in activities of daily living.

title: Hydration-Driven Self-Strengthening Silk Fibroin Ionic Elastomer for Electro-Immunomodulatory Achilles Tendon Repair.
abstract: Achilles tendon repair remains limited by fibrotic healing and implants' inability to coordinate mechanical support, ionic signaling, electrical cues, and immune remodeling in wet load-bearing environments. We report a bioinspired self-strengthening silk fibroin ionic elastomer (SFIE) as an electro-immunomodulatory artificial Achilles tendon. Lithium chloride is integrated into regenerated silk fibroin to create a hydration-responsive protein-ion network. Upon water uptake, LiCl-associated hydration may facilitate chain mobility and the reorganization of hydrophobic silk domains into β-sheet nanocrystals, enhancing tensile strength and modulus while preserving extensibility, fatigue resistance, and ionic conductivity. SFIE sustains Li+ release within a bioactive window that supports bone marrow mesenchymal stem cell (BMSC) viability and tenogenic activity. Mechanistically, SFIE-derived Li+ is associated with altered BMSC paracrine signaling, including reduced arachidonic acid secretion, which may modulate macrophage inflammatory responses. These effects are associated with changes in cPLA2/DUSP3/p38-related signaling. With electrical stimulation, SFIE increases intracellular Ca2 + levels and is associated with changes in CaM/CREB/NR4A1/LIF-related signaling and reduced CXCL10 secretion, potentially contributing to altered macrophage recruitment. In a rat Achilles tendon defect model, SFIE plus electrical stimulation improves gait recovery, tendon continuity, collagen alignment, tendon-marker expression, and local immune remodeling. This work establishes a self-strengthening ionic protein elastomer for functional tendon repair.

title: Scar Treatments in Hand Surgery.
abstract: Scar formation after hand surgery poses unique functional and aesthetic challenges because of the hand's complex anatomy, dense sensory innervation, and reliance on supple skin and tendon glide. Hypertrophic scars, keloids, adherent scars, and contractures can cause pain, hypersensitivity, restricted motion, and impaired activities of daily living, yet evidence guiding scar management in hand surgery remains limited and largely extrapolated from burn and general surgical populations. This review synthesizes current evidence on the biology, classification, prevention, and treatment of scars as they pertain to hand surgery. Nonoperative management, including silicone gel sheeting, compression therapy, intralesional corticosteroid injection, laser therapy, and hand therapy, forms the foundation of care. Operative interventions, ranging from scar excision and Z-plasty to skin grafting, local flap reconstruction, dermal substitutes, and tenolysis, address established contracture and adhesion when conservative measures fail. Emerging therapies, such as autologous fat grafting, growth factor modulation, platelet-rich plasma, and botulinum toxin A, show early promise but require validation in hand-specific trials. Optimal outcomes depend on a collaborative, individualized approach integrating patient risk stratification, meticulous surgical technique, and close coordination with hand therapy throughout the care continuum.

title: Obturator internus muscle entrapment in posterior wall acetabular fractures: two cases with preoperative and intraoperative findings.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: We report two cases of the rare presentation of obturator internus muscle (OI) entrapment in posterior wall fractures of the acetabulum. Although piriformis muscle entrapment has been previously reported, to the best of our knowledge, OI entrapment associated with posterior wall acetabular fractures has not been previously documented.
CASE PRESENTATION: Case 1: A 38-year-old male presented with right hip and knee pain following a road traffic accident. He was diagnosed with a posterior hip dislocation, posterior wall and posterior column fractures of the acetabulum, and a posterior knee dislocation. During surgery, the OI muscle was found interposed between the displaced posterior wall fragment and the remaining posterior column. Case 2: A 43-year-old male sustained blunt abdominal trauma and a Pipkin type IV injury involving a femoral head fracture associated with a posterior wall acetabular fracture following a road traffic accident. After stabilisation of the abdominal injury with laparoscopic repair of the mesenteric injury, the patient underwent open reduction and internal fixation of the posterior wall fracture, along with removal of intra-articular fragments associated with an infra-foveal femoral head fracture. Intraoperatively, the OI muscle was similarly found interposed between the displaced posterior wall fragment and the remaining posterior column. In both cases, retrospective review of the preoperative CT images demonstrated OI interposition corresponding to the intraoperative findings. Both patients followed a standard postoperative rehabilitation protocol. At the one-year follow-up, both patients had satisfactory clinical outcomes, with Merle d'Aubigné-Postel scores of 16 and 17 and Harris Hip Scores of 92.7 and 93 for Cases 1 and 2, respectively. Neither patient showed radiographic evidence of post-traumatic arthritis.
CONCLUSION: These cases highlight the importance of recognising OI muscle entrapment as a potential cause of difficulty in reducing posterior wall acetabular fractures. Careful evaluation of preoperative CT images, particularly using soft-tissue window settings, may facilitate the identification of OI interposition. Intraoperatively, failure to identify the OI tendon between the superior and inferior gemelli, when both are clearly identified, should raise suspicion of entrapment. Meticulous identification of soft-tissue structures may help achieve anatomical fracture reduction and successful fixation.

title: Immediate effect of verbal cues on ACL injury relevant Knee loading during 180° and 90° cutting maneuvers in female university soccer and basketball athletes.
abstract: Young female athletes possess a high risk of rupturing their anterior cruciate ligament (ACL). High external peak knee abduction moments (pKAM) are a likely key risk factor for non-contact ACL injuries. The aim of this study was to evaluate the effect of performance-based movement feedback on pKAM during cutting maneuvers in female university athletes. Thirty-four female university soccer and basketball athletes completed preplanned 180° and 90° cutting trials while ground reaction forces and kinematics were simultaneously captured. Participants immediately received verbal cues targeting foot strike angle, foot progression angle, or trunk lean angle based on their performance. Athletes then repeated the trials post-feedback. Changes in pKAM between baseline and post-feedback trials were analyzed. Soccer and basketball athletes who received the FOOTstrike-angle cue significantly reduced pKAM for both cutting tasks (Soccer: 180°; -0.21 Nm/kg, p < 0.01, d = 0.92; 90°; -0.28 Nm/kg, p < 0.01, d = 1.16. Basketball: 180°; -0.07 Nm/kg, p = 0.02, d = 0.76; 90°; -0.30 Nm/kg, p < 0.01, d = 0.82). The FOOTpro-angle cue significantly reduced pKAM during the 180° cut for soccer athletes (-0.10 Nm/kg, p = 0.01, d = 0.60), but not basketball. The TRUNKlean cue did not significantly affect pKAM for either sport. Individual feedback targeting forefoot landings and neutral foot progression angles can elicit immediate technique change and reduce ACL injury relevant knee loading during cutting maneuvers.

title: Case Study Insights Into Female World-Class and Elite Athletes' Training and Physiology.
abstract:
PURPOSE: This article offers a structured overview of published case studies involving elite and world-class female Olympic athletes, highlighting the unique insights these studies provide into training characteristics, physiology, performance, and female-specific factors.
METHODS: Four databases were systematically searched for peer-reviewed case studies involving tiers 4 to 5 female Olympic athletes reporting individual-level data on training, physiological, and/or performance characteristics.
RESULTS: Thirty-eight studies describing 54 elite and world-class female athletes from 18 countries and 19 Olympic sports met the inclusion criteria. Most studies were published after 2017 (68%), originated from Europe (58%), and involved endurance sports (81%). Fifteen studies examined long-term athlete development, with observation periods ranging from 4 to 26 years. Fourteen studies reported annual training and physiological characteristics across 10 sports including training volume, intensity distribution, periodization, and physiological profiling. Four studies examined altitude training, 8 addressed competition demands, tapering, and precompetition strategies, and 8 focused on female-specific physiology, health, and performance, including energy availability, menstrual function, hormonal cycle monitoring and pregnancy, and postpartum return to sport.
CONCLUSION: Case studies provide unique athlete-centered insights into the complex interactions between training, physiology, health, and performance in elite female athletes. Collectively, they demonstrate that pathways to world-class performance are highly individualized, while generating hypotheses that complement group-based research. Future case studies should prioritize underrepresented sports, geographical regions, and female-specific topics to expand the diversity of performance environments and athlete populations represented in the literature.
journal: International journal of sports physiology and performance

title: Effects of Combined Sprint and Plyometric Training vs Plyometric Training only on Physical Fitness and Sport-Specific Performance in Male Pubertal Soccer Players.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sprint (ST) and plyometric training (PT) are well-established methods for improving physical fitness and sport-specific performance in youth athletes. However, the effects of their combination remain unclear.
AIM: This study investigated the effects of an 8-week combined ST and PT program (SPT), PT-only program, and active control (CG) on physical fitness and sport-specific performance in young male soccer players.
METHODS: Forty-six pubertal Tier 2 training and performance caliber, male soccer players (13.9-14.2 years; maturity offset = 0.18-0.78 years from peak height velocity) participated in the study. Training was conducted twice weekly (2 × 30 min) over 8 weeks and was integrated into regular soccer sessions. The SPT program consisted of a progressive sequence of plyometric exercises (countermovement, line, drop jumps, and single-leg jumps/push-offs), immediately followed by a prescribed 10-15-m sprint or change-of-direction (CoD) task. The PT group performed the same plyometric exercises and exercise order without the subsequent sprint or CoD component. Training loads were monitored using the OMNI 0-10 RPE scale. The CG continued their regular soccer-specific training. Assessments included dynamic balance, muscle strength (reactive strength) and power (standing long jump, countermovement jump, five-jump test), speed (10-m and 30-m linear sprints), CoD speed with and without the ball, and sport-specific performance (throw-in and standing-kick tests).
RESULTS: Significant group × time interactions were observed for most outcomes (p < 0.05), with partial eta-squared (ηp2) values ranging from 0.33 to 0.81. Significant interactions were found for dynamic balance (ηp2 = 0.66), reactive strength (ηp2 = 0.33), power (ηp2 = 0.65-0.81), 10-m sprint performance (ηp2 = 0.42), CoD speed (ηp2 = 0.44-0.45), and sport-specific performance (ηp2 = 0.73-0.78). Bonferroni-adjusted between-group comparisons indicated significant differences between SPT and PT for selected outcomes, including dynamic balance, power (five-jump and countermovement jump tests), speed (10-m sprint and 15-m CoD without the ball), and throw-in performance, whereas no significant SPT-PT differences were detected for the remaining outcomes. Significant pre-post-improvements were observed across the assessed outcomes in the SPT group, while PT also produced significant improvements in several measures and the CG showed limited or non-significant changes. Although both SPT and PT significantly improved 30-m sprint performance, the group × time interaction did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.060, ηp2 = 0.12).
CONCLUSIONS: An 8-week combined SPT intervention was associated with greater performance than PT alone for selected physical fitness and sport-specific outcomes, particularly dynamic balance, power and throw-in performance, in pubertal male Tier 2 soccer players. However, these benefits were outcome-specific and were not observed across all assessed measures.

title: 3D Biomechanics of Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries in Football: What We Have Learned in the Last Five Years.
abstract: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rupture is among the most impacting injuries in professional football. Understanding these injuries in their environment, and their biomechanical mechanism, is the bottleneck between injury surveillance and effective mechanism-informed prevention and rehabilitation. We reconstructed the three-dimensional kinematics of 33 cases of ACL injury sustained by elite male football players during official matches. The Model-Based Image-Matching technique was leveraged to obtain quantitative, detailed estimates of three-dimensional joint kinematics, thereby overcoming the limitations of traditional bidimensional video analyses. This paper reviews and interprets findings derived from over five years of research on the topic from a novel perspective. At the knee level, ACL injury mechanics involved a sequence of multiplanar joint rotations; on the sagittal plane, knee flexion increased from initial contact to injury frame; on the frontal plane, a knee abduction (valgus) shift emerged; on the transverse plane, following ground contact, we observed a sequence of internal and then external rotation of the femur, relative to the tibia, occurring during loading acceptance. Expanding the analysis on total-body kinematics, marked inter-individual variability was observed across the studied cohort; while ACL failure exhibits consistent kinematic features at the knee level, the sequence of whole-body postures leading to injury appears to be context-dependent. Finally, we propose biomechanically informed approaches to injury mitigation, emphasizing the integration of sport-specific contextual determinants, perceptual and decision-making processes, challenging the traditional separation between technical coaching and injury prevention.

title: Post-Exercise Thermal Interventions and Nocturnal Sleep in Athletes: A Narrative Review of the Potential Underlying Physiological Mechanisms.
abstract: Sleep is essential for optimal performance and recovery in athletes. Post-exercise cold exposure, including cold water immersion and cryotherapy, is typically used to enhance recovery, but its effects on sleep remain unclear. Emerging evidence also suggests that post-exercise heat exposure, including sauna and hot water immersion before sleep may improve both objective and subjective sleep outcomes. However, the effectiveness of post-exercise thermal interventions for improving nocturnal sleep in athletes specifically has not yet been comprehensively evaluated. This narrative review synthesizes the current evidence and discusses the potential physiological mechanisms by which post-exercise thermal interventions may influence nocturnal sleep in athletes. Despite methodological heterogeneity, existing research indicates that post-exercise thermal interventions may influence the subsequent nocturnal sleep of athletes through multiple and varying interacting mechanisms. For example, cold exposure close to bedtime (< 2 h) may disrupt sleep by reducing the distal-to-proximal skin temperature gradient (DPG), thereby increasing sleep onset latency and shortening sleep duration. In contrast, when applied more than 2 h before bedtime, cold exposure may improve sleep by augmenting parasympathetic tone and/or reducing muscle soreness and associated nocturnal movement. Although it remains unclear whether post-exercise heat exposure improves sleep via autonomic modulation or reduced muscle soreness, existing evidence indicates that sleep may be facilitated by an increased DPG. Moderating factors such as sex, time of day, environmental temperature, bedding microclimate, acclimatization status, and training load may influence the effects of post-exercise thermal interventions on sleep and should be investigated in future studies.

title: Subject-Specific Cardiovascular Signatures Revealed by Arterial Pulse Signals in Patients with Heart Diseases-Part I: General Cases.
abstract: Background/Objectives: This study evaluates whether cardiovascular (CV) parameters derived from noninvasive arterial pulse signals can capture subject-specific physiological characteristics and longitudinal changes in patients with diverse heart diseases. Method: Arterial pulse signals at the radial artery (RA) and carotid artery (CA) of each patient were successfully recorded from all 18 patients using micro-fabricated tactile sensors. Signal quality was screened before analysis, and the accepted signals were analyzed using a single-degree-of-freedom time-frequency (SDOF-TF) framework. Key CV parameters, including time-based indices-heart rate (HR), heart rate variability (HRV), respiration rate (RR), and respiration modulation (RM), as well as harmonic amplitudes and normalized arterial pulse waveform (APW)-were extracted from measurements at rest and post-exercise across three rehabilitation visits in 18 patients with heterogeneous CV conditions. Longitudinal changes in CV parameters within subjects and variability between subjects were assessed. Results: Compared with a healthy reference, the patients exhibited heterogeneous CV profiles, with lower HRV in all patients except one with AF, who showed elevated HRV, and generally reduced post-exercise CV responses. Higher-order harmonic amplitudes were attenuated at the RA, while CA-derived APW measurements showed greater sensitivity to systolic upstroke slope. Marked inter-subject variability was evident in at-rest CV parameters and 5-min post-exercise responses. Longitudinal CV responses varied across rehabilitation visits, potentially reflecting multiple contributing factors. Conclusions: The 100% pulse acquisition rate supports the feasibility of the tactile sensor technology for pulse measurement, and the combined sensor technology and SDOF-TF framework enable quantitative characterization of shared and individualized CV patterns in cardiac patients and their post-exercise recovery, including time-based indices, harmonic signatures, site-specific differences, and interactions among CV parameters. These findings warrant further investigation in larger cohorts with appropriate physiological reference measurements.

title: The impact of mindfulness on sleep, cognitive function and athletic performance of young males migrating to the plateau.
abstract:
AIMS: To examine whether an 8-week mindfulness training program was associated with changes in sleep quality, cognitive function, and athletic performance in young men who migrated to high-altitude regions.
METHODS: Ninety-six young male migrants were randomly assigned to an 8-week mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT) program (n = 48) or a no-intervention control group (n = 48). Sleep quality (PSQI), cognitive processing (P300 latency), and athletic performance (3000-m run time) were assessed before and after the intervention.
RESULTS: The mindfulness group was associated with greater improvements in sleep quality (PSQI median: 7.5 to 5 vs. 8 to 8.5, P < 0.001) and cognitive processing speed (P300 latency median: 387 ms to 357 ms vs. 376.5 ms to 374.5 ms, P = 0.01) compared with controls. Exploratory analyses suggested that P300 amplitude increased in parietal and occipital regions. No significant between-group difference was observed in 3000-m run completion time (P = 0.51) or grade improvement rates (25.0% vs. 29.17%, P = 0.65).
CONCLUSION: An 8-week mindfulness intervention was associated with improved sleep quality and cognitive processing speed, but no significant association was observed with athletic performance, in young male migrants to high-altitude regions. These preliminary findings suggest potential benefits of mindfulness as a non-pharmacological strategy for high-altitude health management, pending replication with active control conditions.

title: Changes in energy availability, nutritional status, and physiological health across training phases in elite Chinese artistic swimmers.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Low energy availability (LEA) adversely affects athletes'physiological health, yet studies in elite synchronized swimmers across different pre-competition training phases are scarce. This study evaluated changes in energy availability, nutritional status, and physiological health in Chinese elite female synchronized swimmers before the National Games.
METHODS: Ten Chinese elite female synchronized swimmers sequentially completed a 1-week tapering phase (TP) and a 4-week intensified training phase (ITP). At the end of each phase, dietary intake (weighed food records), exercise energy expenditure (heart rate monitoring), energy availability (EA), resting metabolic rate (RMR), body composition, and blood biomarkers were measured. Within each training phase, athletes were classified into LEA and non-LEA groups according to their EA levels, and between-group differences were compared. In addition, overall changes between TP and ITP were analyzed in the full cohort of 10 athletes.
RESULTS: LEA prevalence was 40% during the TP and 60% during the ITP. In unadjusted analyzes, the LEA group showed significantly lower EI (p = 0.025), VO₂ (p = 0.022), mRMR (p = 0.023), RMR ratio (p = 0.006), and intakes of carbohydrate (p = 0.023), protein (p = 0.015), fat (p = 0.032), calcium (p = 0.038), and iron (p = 0.044) during the TP, with large effect-size estimates. As expected from the classification criteria, EA was significantly lower in the LEA group during both the TP (p = 0.001) and ITP (p = 0.005). During the ITP, fat (p = 0.027) and zinc intakes (p = 0.036) were significantly lower in the LEA group, whereas carbohydrate and protein intakes were lower but did not reach statistical significance. In the overall cohort, EEE (p < 0.001) and T4 (p = 0.010) increased from TP to ITP, whereas ferritin (p = 0.012) and calcium intake (p = 0.007) decreased, with large effect-size estimates.
CONCLUSION: During intensified training, EEE increased without a corresponding increase in EI, suggesting that dietary intake may not have adequately matched the increased training demands and may have increased susceptibility to LEA. LEA was associated with lower energy and macronutrient intakes, potential calcium and iron inadequacies, and phase-specific reductions in RMR-related measures. Phase-related biomarker changes could not be attributed specifically to LEA. Individualized and periodized nutritional monitoring and intervention are recommended to better align energy and nutrient intake with training demands and support athlete health and performance.

title: Dysphagia as the Initial Manifestation of Anti-HMGCR Antibody-Positive Immune-Mediated Necrotizing Myopathy Complicated by Pulmonary Embolism.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anti-3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A reductase (anti-HMGCR) antibody-positive immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (IMNM) is a rare autoimmune myopathy characterized by progressive proximal muscle weakness and markedly elevated creatine kinase levels. Although commonly associated with prior statin exposure, statin-naïve cases and atypical presentations are well described. Patients with idiopathic inflammatory myopathies are also at increased risk for venous thromboembolism (VTE), though data specific to IMNM remain limited.
CASE PRESENTATION: An 83-year-old man with brief, remote statin exposure presented with progressive proximal muscle weakness and a three-year history of oropharyngeal dysphagia preceding limb involvement. Laboratory evaluation revealed markedly elevated creatine kinase and transaminases. Anti-HMGCR antibodies were positive, and muscle biopsy confirmed necrotizing myopathy. During evaluation for occult malignancy, bilateral pulmonary emboli were incidentally identified. The patient required high-dose corticosteroids, mycophenolate mofetil, and intravenous immunoglobulin for refractory disease. With aggressive immunosuppressive therapy and rehabilitation, he demonstrated substantial clinical recovery at 6 months.
CONCLUSION: This case highlights oropharyngeal dysphagia as an early and, for a prolonged period, isolated manifestation of anti-HMGCR antibody-positive IMNM; here, it preceded the onset of limb weakness by approximately 3 years. It underscores the importance of comprehensive diagnostic evaluation in patients with unexplained oropharyngeal dysfunction, in whom an inflammatory myopathy may otherwise be overlooked for years. Clinicians should maintain awareness of thrombotic risk in inflammatory myopathies, particularly during active disease. Early recognition and prompt immunosuppressive therapy remain critical to optimize outcomes and prevent irreversible muscle damage.
